name: Living Hall, Picturesque
description: A large hall that is a room rather than a passage, with the stair rising through it, a hearth in an inglenook off it, and the principal rooms opening from it directly - all wrapped in a deliberately irregular, dominated mass. The move that makes it is the inversion of the Georgian idea: where a centre passage is circulation you pass through to reach rooms, the living hall is the room you occupy, and circulation is what happens at its edges. Everything follows from that. There is no separate parlor because the hall took its job; the stair is furniture rather than plumbing; the upper corridor becomes a gallery open to the hall below; and the plan's irregularity is possible only because no facade has to be symmetrical about a door. The type's own risk is stated in its massing: it requires a dominant mass or it disintegrates into a pile of gables. The great Shingle Style houses run to 7,000 sf and more, with service wings and a servants' stair this list does not model. The range above is what these rooms reach; it was 7,000, of which 96% was reachable -- a near miss, corrected for the same reason as the others rather than left because it is small (OQ 45).

rooms.name: Entrance Porch
rooms.note: Deep and low and often tucked under the main roof rather than applied to the front - the entrance in this type is found rather than announced.

rooms.name: Vestibule
rooms.note: A short lock between the door and the hall. Without it the front door opens directly into the room the family occupies, which is the type's most common planning complaint and the reason the better examples always have one.

rooms.name: Living Hall
rooms.note: The room the whole diagram is named for, and it must be big enough to be furnished as a room and still be walked through - see rooms/hall.json's critical_dimension. A living hall you cannot put a sofa in without blocking a route is a wide corridor with a fireplace.

rooms.name: Inglenook
rooms.note: The hearth alcove off the hall, with built-in seats either side of the fire and usually a low ceiling against the hall's high one. Typed as a sitting-room because the catalogue has no inglenook and this is what it functionally is: a small seated room open to a larger one. Its smallness is the point and it should not be scaled up with the house.

rooms.name: Stair
rooms.note: Rising IN the hall, not in a room of its own - a broad first flight, a landing with a window seat, and the whole thing read as the hall's principal furniture.

rooms.name: Parlor
rooms.note: Optional on purpose. In the fully developed type the hall has absorbed the parlor entirely, and a brief that asks for both is asking for the earlier Queen Anne arrangement rather than the Shingle one.

rooms.name: Veranda
rooms.note: Wrapping the seaward or garden corner and often turning into a round tower-end. It is the reason the type reads as horizontal despite its gables.

rooms.name: Upper Gallery
rooms.note: The upper corridor open to the hall below on one side. This is the type's signature at the upper level and the reason rooms/overlook.json exists as a room distinct from a landing.

scaling.note: This diagram grows by extending wings off the hall rather than by adding bays to a front, which is why the massing catalogue calls it picturesque and why its bay module is loose. The constraint that matters is the massing's own: one mass must stay visibly dominant. Growth that produces two equal gables has destroyed the type even where every room is correct.

trades_away: Symmetry, and any possibility of a composed classical front - the type cannot be given one without ceasing to be itself. It trades away the separate parlor, which a formal brief may want back. It trades acoustic privacy hardest of all: the hall is a two-storey volume with an open gallery around it and bedroom doors onto that gallery, so every sound in the house travels, which is why rooms/overlook.json marks a primary bedroom opening straight onto one as a fault to avoid. And it is expensive per square foot - the irregular plan, the multiple roof intersections and the double-height hall all cost, and none of them is floor area you can furnish.
exemplars: Isaac Bell House, Newport, Rhode Island, McKim Mead & White, 1883 - the canonical living hall
William Watts Sherman House, Newport, H. H. Richardson, 1874
Stoughton House, Cambridge, Massachusetts, H. H. Richardson, 1883
Cragside, Northumberland, Norman Shaw, from 1869 - the British parent of the arrangement
